description: Everyday problems of older adults and the people who support them: retirement, aging in place, technology help, medication, isolation, and scams that target elders.

items.title: Forgetting whether today's pills were taken
items.problem: An hour after breakfast an older adult cannot remember if they already took the morning dose, and either skips it or doubles up.
items.who: seniors on daily medications, especially living alone
items.workaround: weekly pill organizers, sticky notes, calling a family member to ask

items.title: Juggling a dozen prescriptions with different schedules
items.problem: Some pills are twice a day with food, some once at bedtime, some every other day; keeping the whole schedule straight in one's head is overwhelming.
items.workaround: handwritten chart taped to the fridge, multiple pill boxes

items.title: Refills running out on different days
items.problem: Each prescription runs out on a different date so there is a pharmacy trip nearly every week and occasionally a gap with no pills at all.
items.who: seniors and their caregivers managing multiple prescriptions
items.workaround: asking the pharmacist to sync refills, calendar reminders

items.title: Not knowing which pills interact
items.problem: Different specialists prescribe drugs without seeing the full list, and the patient has no easy way to check for dangerous interactions or duplicates.
items.workaround: bringing a bag of pill bottles to appointments, asking the pharmacist

items.title: Unreadable tiny print on pill bottles
items.problem: Dosage instructions and warnings on bottle labels are too small to read, so instructions get guessed at or ignored.
items.workaround: magnifying glass, asking someone to read it aloud

items.title: Adult child cannot verify remote parent's meds
items.problem: A daughter living in another state has no way to confirm her father actually took his heart medication today short of calling and nagging.
items.workaround: daily phone calls, hiring a home aide

items.title: Remembering a new medication side effect timeline
items.problem: After starting a new drug the senior cannot tell whether dizziness started before or after, and has nothing to show the doctor at the follow-up.
items.workaround: vague recollection at the appointment

items.title: Phone updates change the interface overnight
items.problem: A software update moves buttons and changes icons, and a senior who had finally learned the phone is lost again and afraid to touch anything.
items.workaround: waiting for a grandchild to visit, avoiding updates

items.title: Same tech question asked every week
items.problem: Adult children get the same 'how do I send a photo' or 'where did my email go' call repeatedly because the steps are not written down anywhere the parent can find.
items.who: seniors and the family members who act as tech support
items.workaround: phone calls, handwritten instruction sheets that get lost

items.title: Forgotten passwords locking out email and banking
items.problem: Passwords are scribbled in a notebook, half are out of date, and every login attempt ends in a reset loop that requires a code sent to a phone they cannot find.
items.workaround: paper notebooks, reusing one password, calling a child

items.title: Two-factor codes on a device across the room
items.problem: Logging in on the computer requires a code texted to a phone that is charging in another room or has a dead battery, and the code expires before it is entered.
items.who: seniors using online banking and portals
items.workaround: giving up and calling the bank

items.title: Accidentally muting or switching phone settings
items.problem: A stray tap turns on Do Not Disturb, silences the ringer, or enables airplane mode, and the senior misses calls for days without knowing why.
items.workaround: family notices they cannot reach them and drives over

items.title: Video calls that fail to connect with grandchildren
items.problem: The family sets up a video call and the senior cannot find the link, the camera is off, or the audio is muted, and the call becomes a frustrating tech session instead of a visit.
items.workaround: falling back to a voice call

items.title: Remote family cannot see the parent's screen
items.problem: Trying to talk a parent through a problem over the phone is guesswork because the helper cannot see what is on the screen and the parent cannot describe it.
items.who: adult children providing remote tech support
items.workaround: long phone calls, driving over, taking photos of the screen

items.title: Too many apps and icons cluttering the home screen
items.problem: Pre-installed and accidentally downloaded apps crowd the phone so the three apps actually needed are hard to find.
items.workaround: asking a relative to 'clean up the phone'

items.title: Pop-ups and fake virus alerts cause panic
items.problem: A browser pop-up saying the computer is infected looks official and the senior does not know whether to click, call the number, or unplug the machine.
items.workaround: calling family, sometimes calling the scam number

items.title: Distinguishing real bank calls from scam calls
items.problem: A caller claims to be from the bank or Medicare and the senior has no quick way to verify whether the call is genuine before sharing information.
items.workaround: hanging up and calling the number on the card, or complying

items.title: Grandparent scam using a panicked family voice
items.problem: A call claiming a grandchild is in jail or hospital and needs gift cards now creates such urgency that the senior acts before checking with anyone.
items.workaround: family code words, none for most

items.title: Family finds out about the scam too late
items.problem: Large unusual transfers, gift card purchases, or new payees go unnoticed by relatives until thousands of dollars are gone.
items.who: adult children of seniors managing their own finances
items.workaround: asking for joint account access, periodic statement reviews

items.title: Phishing emails that mimic familiar services
items.problem: Emails styled as Amazon, Netflix, or the electric company ask to 'update payment' and the senior cannot tell them from real notices.
items.workaround: forwarding suspicious emails to a child to check

items.title: Robocalls flooding the landline all day
items.problem: The phone rings a dozen times a day with spam, so the senior either stops answering entirely and misses real calls or picks up every scam.
items.who: seniors with landlines or basic phones
items.workaround: unplugging the phone, letting everything go to voicemail

items.title: Recurring subscriptions signed up for unknowingly
items.problem: Free trials, magazine renewals, and 'protection plans' quietly charge the card monthly and the senior does not notice or cannot find how to cancel.
items.who: seniors with credit or debit cards
items.workaround: a relative auditing statements once a year

items.title: Romance scam isolation goes unnoticed
items.problem: A lonely widow forms an online relationship with someone who slowly asks for money, and no one in the family sees the pattern until savings are drained.
items.workaround: none

items.title: Days pass without speaking to anyone
items.problem: A senior living alone can go three or four days without a single conversation, and there is no natural prompt for anyone to reach out.
items.who: seniors living alone, widowed or far from family
items.workaround: television for company, waiting for someone to call

items.title: No one would notice a fall for days
items.problem: If a senior living alone fell in the bathroom, nobody would know until a missed weekly call, which is the fear that keeps both them and their children up at night.
items.who: seniors living alone and their families
items.workaround: daily check-in calls, medical alert pendants they forget to wear

items.title: Daily check-in calls feel like surveillance
items.problem: Children want reassurance that mom is okay each morning, but the daily 'just checking' call feels intrusive to the parent and burdensome to the child.
items.workaround: phone calls, texts that go unanswered and cause panic

items.title: Finding local activities for people their age
items.problem: Senior center schedules, library talks, and walking groups are scattered across paper flyers and church bulletins, so the senior does not know what is on this week.
items.workaround: word of mouth, paper newsletters

items.title: Losing a social circle after retirement
items.problem: Work provided daily contact for forty years; after retiring the calendar is empty and there is no obvious way to meet new people with shared interests.
items.workaround: volunteering, religious groups

items.title: Making new friends after moving to a retirement community
items.problem: New residents do not know who shares their hobbies or who is open to a dinner companion, and dining alone for weeks is common.
items.who: seniors newly moved to retirement or assisted living communities
items.workaround: activities director, trial and error

items.title: Grandchildren's lives only visible on platforms seniors avoid
items.problem: Family photos and updates live on Instagram and group chats the grandparent does not use, so they feel left out of everyday family life.
items.workaround: occasional printed photos, forwarded texts

items.title: No ride to appointments after giving up driving
items.problem: Once a senior stops driving, every doctor visit or grocery run depends on a relative's availability, and rideshare apps are confusing to book.
items.workaround: asking family, expensive taxis, paratransit with long lead times

items.title: Coordinating who drives Mom this week
items.problem: Siblings trade texts trying to figure out who can take their mother to Tuesday's cardiology appointment, and sometimes nobody shows up.
items.who: sibling groups caring for a parent
items.workaround: group text threads, shared spreadsheets

items.title: Siblings out of sync on parent's health updates
items.problem: One sibling attends the appointment and the others hear a garbled second-hand version days later, causing arguments and duplicated calls to the doctor.
items.who: adult siblings sharing care of a parent
items.workaround: group texts, one sibling becomes the sole information hub

items.title: Remembering what the doctor said
items.problem: By the time the senior gets home from the appointment they cannot recall the new instructions, the dosage change, or when the next test is.
items.workaround: bringing a family member, after-visit summary printouts

items.title: Multiple patient portals with separate logins
items.problem: The cardiologist, primary care doctor, and hospital each use a different portal, and finding a lab result means remembering which one and which password.
items.workaround: calling the office instead, ignoring portals entirely

items.title: Preparing questions before a short appointment
items.problem: Symptoms noticed over the past month are forgotten in the ten-minute visit, and the senior leaves without asking the things that worried them.
items.workaround: notes on scrap paper, hoping to remember

items.title: Tracking blood pressure and sugar readings by hand
items.problem: Daily readings are written in a notebook that is hard to summarize, so the doctor gets a pile of numbers rather than a trend.
items.who: seniors monitoring blood pressure, glucose, or weight
items.workaround: paper logs, memory

items.title: Keeping up with Medicare paperwork and deadlines
items.problem: Open enrollment windows, plan changes, and explanation-of-benefits letters arrive constantly, and it is unclear which need action and which are junk.
items.who: seniors on Medicare and their helpers
items.workaround: piles of mail, a knowledgeable relative or SHIP counselor

items.title: Surprise medical bills that may already be paid
items.problem: Bills arrive from labs and hospitals months after the visit, and the senior cannot tell whether insurance covered it, whether they already paid, or whether it is a scam.
items.workaround: paying everything twice, or ignoring bills until collections

items.title: Fear of outliving retirement savings
items.problem: A retiree does not know whether their monthly withdrawals are sustainable and lives with constant anxiety about running out of money at 90.
items.workaround: occasional visits to a financial advisor, rough spreadsheets

items.title: Required minimum distribution deadlines missed
items.problem: Retirees forget to take required withdrawals from retirement accounts by year end and face steep penalties.
items.workaround: brokerage reminder letters, accountant

items.title: Bills paid late after spouse who handled money dies
items.problem: When the partner who always handled finances passes away, the survivor does not know which bills are on autopay, where accounts are, or when things are due.
items.workaround: children step in, rummaging through paper files

items.title: Important documents scattered and unfindable
items.problem: The will, power of attorney, insurance policies, and deed are in different drawers, safe deposit boxes, and lawyers' offices, and nobody knows where.
items.workaround: a binder that is never fully updated

items.title: Empty days with no structure after retiring
items.problem: Without a job the days blur together, motivation drops, and the retiree feels aimless despite wanting to stay active.
items.workaround: part-time work, hobbies picked up haphazardly

items.title: Remembering to eat and drink enough
items.problem: Living alone, a senior skips meals or forgets to drink water all day, leading to dizziness and hospital visits for dehydration.
items.who: seniors living alone with reduced appetite
items.workaround: family reminders, meal delivery programs

items.title: Stove or appliance left on
items.problem: A burner or iron gets left on after a distraction and nobody is around to notice, creating a real fire risk and eroding confidence in living alone.
items.workaround: family removes stove knobs, automatic shutoff devices

items.title: Finding trustworthy home help
items.problem: Hiring someone to clean gutters, fix a railing, or help with bathing means vetting strangers with no easy way to check references or pricing.
items.who: seniors aging in place and their families
items.workaround: word of mouth, church contacts, generic contractor sites

items.title: Assessing what home changes are needed
items.problem: Families do not know which grab bars, lighting, or ramp changes matter most for their parent's home until after a fall.
items.who: families of seniors aging in place
items.workaround: occupational therapist visits if covered, guesswork

items.title: Wandering or getting lost on familiar routes
items.problem: A parent with early dementia takes a walk and does not come back on time, and the family has no way to know where they are.
items.who: families of seniors with cognitive decline
items.workaround: GPS tags, restricting outings

items.title: Emergency info not available to responders
items.problem: When paramedics arrive, the senior's medications, allergies, conditions, and emergency contacts are not accessible in one place.
items.workaround: 'File of Life' on the fridge, medical ID bracelets

items.title: Paid caregivers with no shared handoff notes
items.problem: Morning and evening aides do not know what the other did, whether the senior ate, or how they slept, so problems slip between shifts.
items.workaround: a paper notebook on the kitchen table

items.title: Caregiver burnout with no backup
items.problem: A spouse caring for a partner with dementia has no respite, cannot leave the house, and does not know what help exists or how to schedule it.
items.workaround: none, or adult day programs discovered by chance

items.title: Tracking caregiving expenses for reimbursement or taxes
items.problem: Receipts for prescriptions, supplies, and mileage pile up and cannot be sorted when it is time to split costs among siblings or claim deductions.
items.who: family caregivers paying out of pocket
items.workaround: shoebox of receipts

items.title: Hearing the phone ring or the doorbell
items.problem: Hearing loss means missed calls and missed deliveries, and callers assume the senior is ignoring them or something is wrong.
items.workaround: flashing lights, turning volume to maximum

items.title: Websites and apps with tiny text and low contrast
items.problem: Even with reading glasses, many apps use small gray text on white, so seniors give up on tasks like paying a bill or reading a message.
items.workaround: pinch-zooming, asking someone else to read it

items.title: Remembering birthdays and reaching out
items.problem: As memory slips, the senior forgets grandchildren's birthdays and loses the easy excuses to call, which deepens distance from family.
items.workaround: paper calendar, being reminded by a spouse

items.title: Grocery delivery apps too confusing to use
items.problem: A senior who can no longer carry groceries cannot navigate the delivery app's substitutions, tips, and checkout steps and ends up ordering wrong items or nothing.
items.workaround: a relative places the order for them

items.title: Knowing which day it is and what is scheduled
items.problem: Without work or school routines, days lose their markers and the senior shows up on the wrong day for appointments or misses them.
items.who: retired seniors with mild memory decline
items.workaround: large-print wall calendar, day clocks
